Asthma

severity by day and night symptom counts · the step ladder · exam answer vs current guidelineHow often are the day and night symptoms, and is the answer ladder keyed to the exam or the current guideline?

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Day symptoms, night wakings and FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) set the severity the NAEPP (National Asthma Education and Prevention Program) step: intermittent, a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) alone; persistent, add an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS), then a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA)
  • Spirometry before and after a bronchodilator: FEV1 up >12% asthma; normal spirometry, still suspected methacholine challenge
  • Severe attack: SABA ipratropium systemic steroids oxygen; wheeze fading while hypoxemia persists intubate
What it is

Hyperresponsive airways that narrow reversibly

Driver

Airway inflammation parasympathetic tone bronchoconstriction

Triggers

Allergens (atopic asthma), smoke, irritant fumes, cold air, viral infections, exercise

Aspirin in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease; nonselective beta-blockers

Reflux at night

Chain

Inflamed, twitchy airways reversible narrowing wheeze, cough, tight chest; worse at night as it gets more severe

Severe attack air trapping too little airflow to wheeze hypoxemia, then respiratory failure

Insights

A rescue inhaler used 4 days a week is not intermittent asthma: count the days, then step up to a daily controller

A quiet chest in a tiring patient is air trapping, not recovery

2Urgent risks
Severe attackAcute, severe exacerbation
Every patient: albuterol (SABA) with ipratropium, systemic steroids, oxygen Watch forOral prednisone preferred; intravenous is acceptable. At discharge, prednisone 40 to 60 mg daily for 5 to 7 days lowers relapse and admission.

If there is no improvement after an hour, choose one dose of intravenous magnesium sulfate.

FailingAltered consciousness, cyanosis, saturation <90%, PaO2 (arterial oxygen pressure) <60 mm Hg, PaCO2 (arterial carbon dioxide) >45 mm Hg
Wheeze fades while hypoxemia persists: silent chest from air trapping

If respiratory failure persists despite escalating treatment, choose intubation.

HistoryPast respiratory failure needing ventilation
The single greatest risk factor for a life-threatening attack
3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
AsthmaEpisodic wheeze, cough, tight chest; worse at night; lungs usually normal between attacksUsually before 40; FEV1 up >12% after a bronchodilator
Smoker; productive cough first40s and 50s; partial or no reversal after the bronchodilator
Paradoxical vocal fold motion (vocal cord dysfunction)"Asthma" that fails usual therapy; inspiratory stridor, not expiratory wheezeFlat inspiratory loop; FVC (forced vital capacity) and ratio normal
Chronic dry cough is the main symptom; often at nightNormal spirometry; methacholine challenge
Asthma or cystic fibrosis with eosinophiliaAn IgE-mediated (immunoglobulin E) reaction; worked up in the structural lung brief
Wheeze with progressive dyspnea and orthopneaBilateral crackles and leg edema
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Sickle cell disease with wheezeAsthma: common, and it raises acute chest syndrome riskSpirometry first, as for anyone
Night cough while already on a proton pump inhibitorReflux unlikely; asthmaPulmonary function tests for bronchodilator response
Asthma, nasal polyps, wheeze after aspirinAspirin-exacerbated respiratory diseaseAvoid aspirin and other cyclooxygenase-1 inhibitors

Pause point. The bait: a child who wheezes "only now and then" but reaches for the rescue inhaler 4 days a week. Severity comes from the counts, not the impression, so this is persistent asthma and needs a daily controller.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: asthma Symptoms – episodic wheeze, cough, tight chest · Reversibility – FEV1 up >12% and >200 mL after a bronchodilator
6Severity
NAEPP severity, age 5 and older
ClassDay symptomsNight wakingsFEV1Start
Intermittent≤2 days a week≤2 a month>80%SABA as needed
Mild persistent>2 days a week, not daily3 to 4 a month>80%Add low-dose ICS
Moderate persistentDaily>1 a week, not nightly60 to 80%Low-dose ICS with a LABA, or medium-dose ICS
Severe persistentThroughout the dayOften nightly<60%High-dose ICS with a LABA
In practiceIn practice: UWorld now follows GINA (Global Initiative for Asthma), which supports a short-acting beta-agonist alone at no step, so even intermittent asthma gets an inhaled corticosteroid, as needed with formoterol or with the reliever. Intermittent symptoms still mean ongoing airway inflammation. NBME still keys NAEPP: a ladder of "nothing extra, montelukast, low-dose inhaled corticosteroid, add a long-acting beta-agonist" marks a NAEPP question.
7Treatment
1

Every patientfrom diagnosis

A SABA for quick relief at every step; avoid triggers; a written action plan

Before exercise, the SABA prevents exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.

2

Mildmild persistent

Add a daily low-dose ICS

Montelukast (a leukotriene antagonist) can be added at any step.

3

Moderatemoderate persistent, or not controlled

Low-dose ICS plus a LABA, or a medium-dose ICS

Before any step up: adherence, inhaler technique, triggers, other conditions.

4

Severesevere persistent

High-dose ICS plus a LABA
5

Addstill not controlled

Add oral steroids
First treatment by situation
SituationChooseWatch for
Symptoms only with exerciseA SABA before exercise; not exercise avoidanceDaily symptoms, or the SABA fails: start a controller
A LABA is consideredAlways with an ICSNever a LABA alone Why notAn oral adenosine antagonist kept for its low cost; never the answer on the exam.
PregnancyExpect worsening if asthma was severe or poorly controlledOften in the second trimester
Needs a beta-blockerAvoid nonselective agentsThey worsen asthma
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
Well controlled for 3 months or moreConsider stepping down
Thrush on an ICSA spacer and rinsing the mouth after each dose
Every patientSpirometry at least every 1 to 2 years
Practice
  1. 9 yo M, symptoms 1 day per week, night waking once a month, normal FEV₁ → Intermittent → SABA as needed
  2. 9 yo M, symptoms 4 days per week, 3 nights a month, FEV₁ 85% → Mild persistent → low-dose inhaled corticosteroid
  3. 9 yo M with daily symptoms, weekly night waking, FEV₁ 70% → Moderate persistent → low-dose ICS plus LABA
  4. 9 yo M with symptoms throughout the day, nightly waking, FEV₁ 55% → Severe persistent
  5. 9 yo M using his rescue inhaler four times a week → Step up to a daily controller – this is not intermittent asthma
  6. 9 yo M with symptoms only on exertion, otherwise well → SABA before exercise
